checks.prompt: You already have a Bayesian network library and a Prolog system on the machine. For a domain whose random variables are generated by rules over an entity set that keeps changing, what does a probabilistic logic program give you that neither of those does?
checks.explanation: Rules generate the structure — that is the whole point, and it is what a hand-drawn network cannot follow when the entities change. The last option is the reverse of the truth: independence of the annotated facts is the foundation the semantics is built on.
options: The structure is produced by relational rules rather than drawn by hand, so recursion and a growing set of entities need no new diagram — while the answers are still exact marginals and posteriors, which the logic system on its own cannot produce at all
It removes the need for exact inference, because the rules are compiled into a sampling procedure that scales to any size of model
It handles continuous quantities natively, which the network library does not
It drops the independence assumptions the network library forces on you, so no fact has to be treated as independent of the others

checks.prompt: Two separate rules conclude the same atom, each annotated 0.6. A colleague expects 1.2, sees that this is impossible, and proposes capping the result at 1. Explain what the semantics actually give here, derive the number, and say why the cap is wrong even in cases where it would produce a value below one.
checks.explanation: Once probabilities are read as a measure over worlds rather than as numbers attached to rules, the arithmetic stops being a matter of opinion. Every surprising combination in this language comes back to counting worlds.
checks.expected: A correct answer must state the semantics in terms of POSSIBLE WORLDS: each annotated fact is an independent coin, a world is one truth assignment to all of them whose probability is the product of the per-fact probabilities, and the atom's probability is the total mass of the worlds in which the rules derive it. The derivation must be given: the atom fails only in the single world where both coins fail, so the answer is one minus 0.4 times 0.4, that is 0.84. The critique of the cap must identify the actual error as DOUBLE COUNTING the world in which both hold, not as overflow — and must show it bites below one too, for instance two rules at 0.3 give one minus 0.7 times 0.7, which is 0.51 and not the 0.6 that adding would produce. Naming this combination rule, and noting that the engine gets it right by compiling the proofs into a formula rather than by combining rule probabilities one at a time, is a plus.

checks.prompt: A three-way categorical outcome is needed, where exactly one of the three happens. A colleague writes three separate annotated facts at one third each. What is wrong with that, and what should be written instead?
checks.explanation: Independence is the default and it is a modelling commitment, not a formality: three coins give eight worlds, of which only three are the ones intended. Exclusivity has to be asked for.
options: Independent facts admit worlds in which two or three of the outcomes hold together and worlds in which none does, so the outcome is not exclusive at all — the construct for a single choice among alternatives, with weights summing to at most one, is what this calls for
Nothing is wrong with the marginals; only conditional queries are affected, and then only when the observation mentions two of the three
The three values do not sum to exactly one once rounded, which the engine rejects when the program is loaded
Separate facts may not share a naming prefix, so the three would be collapsed into a single atom by the grounder

checks.prompt: Implement `marginal(probs, holds, evidence=None)` — the semantics computed by brute force. `probs` maps each independent random fact's name to its probability. Enumerate every assignment of those facts to True/False; the weight of one assignment is the product over facts of its probability when True and one minus it when False. `holds(world)` is given a dict of fact name to bool and says whether the query is derived in that world. Return the total weight of the worlds where it holds. When `evidence` is given — the same shape of callable — restrict to the worlds it accepts and return the conditional probability; raise ValueError if those worlds carry no weight at all. An empty `probs` has exactly one world. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Everything the language does is in that sum, which is why two rules for one atom combine the way they do rather than adding — the world where both fire is counted once because it is one world. It is also why exact inference is hard: the loop you wrote is exponential in the number of annotated facts, and the real engine's compilation step is an attempt to avoid enumerating it, not a different definition of the answer.
checks.test:
sprinkler = {"rain": 0.6, "sprinkler": 0.8}
wet = lambda w: w["rain"] or w["sprinkler"]
assert abs(marginal(sprinkler, wet) - 0.92) < 1e-9, marginal(sprinkler, wet)
assert abs(marginal(sprinkler, lambda w: w["rain"]) - 0.6) < 1e-9
assert abs(marginal(sprinkler, lambda w: w["rain"] and w["sprinkler"]) - 0.48) < 1e-9

two = {"a": 0.6, "b": 0.6}
assert abs(marginal(two, lambda w: w["a"] or w["b"]) - 0.84) < 1e-9, "not 1.2, and not 1.0"

assert marginal({}, lambda w: True) == 1.0
assert marginal({}, lambda w: False) == 0.0

med = {"disease": 0.01, "true_positive": 0.90, "false_positive": 0.05}
positive = lambda w: (w["disease"] and w["true_positive"]) or (
    (not w["disease"]) and w["false_positive"])
post = marginal(med, lambda w: w["disease"], evidence=positive)
assert abs(post - 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0495)) < 1e-9, post

sure = marginal(med, lambda w: w["disease"], evidence=lambda w: w["disease"])
assert abs(sure - 1.0) < 1e-9

try:
    marginal(sprinkler, wet, evidence=lambda w: False)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("conditioning on something impossible must not return a number")

checks.prompt: A model that answered in milliseconds over ten entities takes hours over three hundred, with memory climbing steadily and no answer produced at all. What is most likely happening, and what are the two honest responses?
checks.explanation: Memory rising with no answer in sight points at the step before inference, not at inference itself. Both responses are real engineering: shrink what gets instantiated, or give up exactness deliberately.
options: The program is instantiated over all the entities and the resulting structure is built before any probability is computed, and exact inference over it is intractable in general — either cut the program down to the part the query actually depends on, or move to approximate inference
Probabilities are recomputed from scratch for each query, so caching results between queries removes the growth
The recursion stops being stratified at that size, and the engine falls back on an exhaustive search that stratifying would avoid
The per-world probabilities underflow, forcing a switch to arbitrary-precision arithmetic, which is where the time goes

checks.prompt: Three modelling problems land together. (a) A hierarchical regression on continuous measurements from forty clinics. (b) Predicting missing links in a knowledge graph where the rules are already known and are recursive. (c) The same as (b), except the underlying facts come from a classifier reading scanned documents. Assign each to a tool and justify it by the SHAPE of the uncertainty rather than by the size of the problem.
checks.explanation: Continuous, discrete-relational and perceptual are three different kinds of not-knowing, and each has a family of tools built for it. Sizing the problem tells you which engine within a family; the shape tells you which family.
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all three and justify each by the kind of uncertainty. (a) belongs to a general-purpose probabilistic programming language with gradient-based sampling: the quantities are CONTINUOUS and hierarchical, and this family of languages is discrete-only, so it is the wrong shape rather than merely a slower one. (b) is the home case: DISCRETE, RELATIONAL and RECURSIVE with the rules already in hand, which is exactly what a distribution over possible worlds generated by rules is for — and a hand-built network cannot express it compactly because the structure follows from the rules over a changing entity set. (c) calls for the neural-symbolic extension: the logic and the inference are unchanged, but the annotated facts are produced by a perceptual model instead of being fixed constants, and the model is trained through the inference. Noting that (b) is where the instantiation blow-up bites at scale, so approximate inference may be forced, and that with every probability equal to one this reduces to ordinary logic programming, are pluses.
